newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Troubles far from over for Albania's Berisha.
newsitem.headline: Troubles far from over for Albania's Berisha.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha has little room to manoeuvre, politically or economically, to quell the fury of investors left destitute by a savings scheme collapse -- and his troubles appear far from over.

The president, who must stand for re-election in a parliamentary vote next week, is no longer totally in command of his ruling Democratic Party after 12 deputies demanded the government's resignation over the financial scandal.
Since the Democrats won 122 seats in the 140-member assembly in last year's disputed general election, Berisha is almost certain to win a second term even without the backing of the 12 dissidents.

But over the past five years he has been deserted by senior liberals who co-founded the Democrats in December 1990 but have since joined opposition parties or left Albania altogether. New cracks within the party could leave him even more isolated.

"There is definite unease inside the Democratic Party," one Albanian political writer told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity. "There is also a feeling that more deputies could join the 12 if the current crisis is not solved quickly."
Thousands of people took to the streets in protest after learning they had lost their savings in the pyramid schemes, demanding the government's resignation and their money back.
For Berisha, the first demand is dangerous, the second impossible.
Sacking Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and his government could spell political suicide during the current instability.

"I don't see a government dismissal in the near term. It could bring down the whole house of cards," a senior Western diplomat said. "Once President Berisha is re-elected, he may move to call early elections later in the year which is what many countries in the West would like to see."
The symbolism of mounting student anger across the Balkan state is not lost on Berisha or his Democrats.
It was students who stirred up the uprising that toppled more than four decades of Stalinist rule in 1990, and students who helped found the Democratic Party.
Politics aside, Berisha, a monetarist, is facing more immediate economic problems. He has repeatedly told Albanians his government cannot pay back savers.
He is right. State coffers are empty and Europe's most impoverished nation ran a budget deficit last year of $260 million, or nearly nine percent of gross domestic product.
The spectre of hyper-inflation looms, with prices already on the rise at a time when thousands are suffering financially.
Bread, the scarcity of which sparked riots in 1991 in which 40 people died, costs 50 percent more than last July following a price liberalisation law. Fuel has gone the same way.

Albania's central bank on Thursday quoted the local currency, the lek, at 142 to the U.S. dollar, a plunge of around 35 percent from the beginning of January. On the street, the dollar is selling at around 150 leks.
Savers who managed to scrape back some cash from the collapsed pyramid funds, and other investors are desperate to convert their leks into dollars, fuelling the lek weakness.
John King, the International Monetary Fund's representative in Tirana, said the body was willing to help Albania out.
"IMF assistance will be given to the central bank to improve currency reserves...but there will be conditions," King told the independent daily Koha Jone in an interview.
Independent Albanian analysts said the IMF might demand significant cuts in the public sector workforce and that could force up already high unemployment and fuel more anger.

Violent clashes between demonstrators and police have abated but one Tirana political analyst said protests could resume by the end of March or April, as other savings schemes were likely to begin to crumble.

Thousands of people with cash invested in five other savings funds, including the biggest scheme in Vefa Holdings, are still hoping they will get back all their capital, estimated to amount to millions of dollars.
But analysts doubt all the money will be available.
"While there is still hope, it will remain calm. But the figures don't add up and I have to agree that there could be fresh trouble," a Western diplomat said.
